title: What violence prevention training must New Jersey hospitals and nursing homes provide?
seoTitle: New Jersey health care violence training
description: N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11: annual violence prevention training of at least two hours for all hospital and nursing home workers, nine topics, five-year records.
shortAnswer: New Jersey's Violence Prevention in Health Care Facilities rules, N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11, require licensed general, special and psychiatric hospitals and nursing homes to train all health care workers, including supervisors, managers and security staff, regardless of risk level. Training must happen initially and then annually, last at least two hours on paid work time, use at least two methods and cover nine topics. Training records are kept for five years.
keyTakeaways: The rules apply to general hospitals, special hospitals, county and private psychiatric hospitals and nursing homes licensed under N.J.S.A. 26:2H-1 et seq.
Every health care worker directly employed by the facility must be trained annually, "regardless of their level of risk," with interim training for people who start between annual sessions.
Each session must be at least two hours long, held during paid work time, and use at least two methods such as handouts, discussion, role playing or computer-based activities.
Training must be offered in any language that is the exclusive language of at least 10 percent of the facility's health care workers.
A violence prevention committee, at least half direct-care workers, must review training content and methods every year and meet at least quarterly.
regulator: New Jersey Department of Health (NJDOH), health care facility licensure
appliesTo: General hospitals, special hospitals, county and private psychiatric hospitals licensed under N.J.S.A. 26:2H-1 et seq.
Nursing homes licensed under N.J.S.A. 26:2H-1 et seq.
All health care workers directly employed by a covered facility, including supervisors, managers and security staff

sections.heading: Which New Jersey facilities must run a violence prevention program?

blocks.text: Licensed hospitals of several types and nursing homes must. N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.1 applies the subchapter, titled Violence Prevention in Health Care Facilities, to "general hospitals, special hospitals, county and private psychiatric hospitals and nursing homes" licensed under P.L. 1971, c. 136 (N.J.S.A. 26:2H-1 et seq.) The rules sit in chapter 43E, the general licensure standards for all licensed facilities, and are enforced by the New Jersey Department of Health through the licensure penalties in N.J.A.C. 8:43E-3.

A "health care worker" is "an individual who is directly employed by a covered health care facility." Violence includes "any physical assault or any physical or credible verbal threat of assault or harm" against a health care worker, where a credible verbal threat must be corroborated by independent evidence and cause a reasonable belief of imminent threat of death or serious bodily injury. The rules still refer to the former Department of Health and Senior Services; the current agency is the New Jersey Department of Health.
Facilities had to establish a program by December 6, 2011, and the committee had to produce a written plan by March 6, 2012. This page states the position as at November 2026.

sections.heading: What does N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.10 require for training?

blocks.text: It requires initial training within three months after the violence prevention plan is developed and annual training after that "for all health care workers, including supervisors, managers and security staff, regardless of their level of risk." New Jersey is unusual in setting both a minimum length and a minimum number of methods.

blocks.text: The two-hour minimum is per training, so a facility cannot meet the annual requirement with a 20-minute refresher. The "regardless of their level of risk" wording also rules out limiting training to emergency or psychiatric units; dietary, housekeeping and administrative staff are included. See [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: What must the training content include?

blocks.text: Subsection (g) sets nine minimum content areas. Two of them depend on the facility's own data, so a purchased course cannot cover the whole requirement.

items: Requirements of the workplace violence rules in the subchapter.
A review of the facility's relevant policies.
Techniques to de-escalate and minimize violent behavior.
Appropriate responses to workplace violence, including the use of restraining techniques.
Location and operation of safety devices.
A summary and analysis of the facility's risk factors identified in the violence risk assessment, and preventive actions taken in response.
Information on multicultural diversity to increase staff sensitivity to racial and ethnic issues and differences.

blocks.text: Item 8 means the training must change each year with the annual risk assessment. Item 6 is site specific: the location of panic alarms and duress devices differs by building and unit. The committee must carry out "Development, annual review, evaluation and revision of violence prevention training content and methods," so a committee record of that review is part of the evidence. See [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change).

sections.heading: How do the committee and risk assessment shape training?

blocks.text: The violence prevention committee owns the training content and the risk assessment that feeds it. Under N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.4, the committee must meet at least quarterly, include a representative of administration responsible for the program, and have at least 50 percent of members who are health care workers with direct patient or resident contact. Where workers are unionized, administration must consult the collective bargaining agents on selecting worker members.

N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.7 requires an annual violence risk assessment for each facility that considers OSHA's Guidelines for Preventing Workplace Violence for Health Care and Social Service Workers (the rule cites the 2004 edition, OSHA 3148-2004, "as amended and supplemented"; OSHA now publishes the 2016 revision, OSHA 3148-06R). The assessment includes a job task analysis for each health care worker and annual walk-through surveys of all worksite areas by at least two committee members, one of them a direct care staff member.

Health care systems with more than one covered facility may run the program and committee at system level under N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.5, but they must include at least one direct care worker from each facility, produce a plan for each facility, and keep each facility's data distinct. Training content item 8 must still reflect the specific facility.

sections.heading: What records must be kept, and who can see them?

blocks.text: Training records must be kept for at least five years after the reported act, as one of 12 record types listed in N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.12 that relate to violent acts. Others include incident investigation reports, the NJOSH 300 and OSHA 300 logs, workers' compensation records, police reports and minutes of safety meetings.

The Department of Health must have immediate access to these records. An employee and their authorized representatives must have access to the employee's identifiable records and to de-identified or aggregated data within two business days. Separately, N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.9 requires a copy of the plan to be given to any health care worker or collective bargaining agent within two business days of a request, translated where the 10 percent language threshold is met, with security-sensitive information removed. See [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).
N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.14 prohibits retaliatory action against any health care worker for reporting violent incidents, so the reporting module should state that protection plainly.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry separates the fixed content areas from the facility-specific ones, so the annual risk assessment summary and safety device locations are updated for each facility while the shared content stays stable. Session length, methods and language are recorded with each completion. See [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences).

faqs.q: Can New Jersey hospital violence training be completed online?
faqs.a: Computer-based training is one permitted method, but N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.10 requires at least two methods, such as computer-based activities plus discussion or role playing. Each training must also last at least two hours during paid work time.

faqs.q: Do non-clinical staff need violence prevention training in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Yes. The rule requires training for all health care workers, including supervisors, managers and security staff, regardless of their level of risk. A health care worker is anyone directly employed by the covered facility.

faqs.q: Do the New Jersey rules apply to assisted living or home health agencies?
faqs.a: Subchapter 11 applies to general hospitals, special hospitals, county and private psychiatric hospitals and nursing homes licensed under N.J.S.A. 26:2H-1 et seq. Other facility types are not listed in its scope section.

faqs.q: How long must violence prevention training records be kept?
faqs.a: N.J.A.C. 8:43E-11.12 lists training records among the documents that must be maintained for at least five years after the reported act, with immediate access for the Department of Health.
